lead: The Church-Turing thesis says that every function a human can compute by a finite, exact, mechanical procedure can also be computed by a Turing machine. It matters because it turns the informal word 'algorithm' into a formal object you can analyse. It is used to justify writing an algorithm instead of a full tape-level Turing machine, and to upgrade 'no Turing machine decides this' into 'no algorithm decides this'. The evidence is that lambda calculus, recursive functions and Post systems all define exactly the same class of functions as Turing machines. It is a thesis, not a theorem.
prereq: You need 5.1 and 5.3: how a Turing machine runs, and how integer functions are encoded on its tape.

blocks.text: A Turing machine computes an integer function when you start it with the input encoded on the tape, let it run, and it halts with the output encoded on the tape. Chapter 5.3 gives the unary encoding. The function is the rule that maps each input to that output.

The thesis needs one more idea. A function is effectively computable if a person can compute it by following a finite list of exact instructions, using unlimited paper and pencil, and stop in finite time. The instructions must need no insight or guessing. This is an informal idea, not a mathematical definition.
f is effectively computable ⇒ some Turing machine computes f
blocks.where: f is a function from natural-number inputs to a natural-number output; the arrow means 'implies'.

blocks.text: The Church-Turing thesis states that the implication is always true. Every effectively computable function is computable by a Turing machine. An equivalent form says every reasonable model of mechanical computation computes exactly the Turing-computable functions. Some syllabi call it Church's thesis or the Turing hypothesis.
Three independent formal models were built in the same era. Each tried to capture mechanical calculation, and each used a different mechanism.

items: Lambda calculus: terms are built from variables, application and abstraction; computation is substitution and reduction.
Recursive functions: functions are built from zero, successor and projection, then closed under composition, primitive recursion and minimization.
Post systems: a computation is a sequence of string rewrites using fixed rules.
Turing machines: a computation is a sequence of tape reads, writes and head moves.

blocks.text: These models look unrelated. Lambda calculus reduces expressions. Recursive functions build numbers. Post systems rewrite strings. Turing machines move a head. Yet each defines exactly the same class of functions: the Turing-computable functions.

The convergence is strong evidence. A result that one model equals Turing machines is a theorem, proved by simulation. The thesis is the further claim that this class is the whole of effective computability. No routine calculation has been found outside the class.

A theorem is proved from formal definitions. The Church-Turing thesis relates a formal model to an informal idea. 'Effectively computable' has no formal definition independent of the models. So no proof can compare the two in the way a theorem is proved.

We can prove that lambda calculus and Turing machines define the same functions. That is a theorem about two formal systems. It does not prove that every possible intuitive procedure is covered. One example, or one model, cannot prove the thesis. Evidence is broad: many independent models agree, and generations of algorithms have been simulated by Turing machines.

Use the thesis in two directions. To show a function is computable, give a finite mechanical procedure; the thesis says a Turing machine exists. To show a problem has no algorithm, show no Turing machine decides it; the thesis turns that into 'no effective procedure decides it'. Unit 6 uses this for undecidability.

The thesis is about what can be computed, not how fast. A language or chip is called Turing-complete when it can simulate a Turing machine. That says nothing about running time or memory. Efficiency belongs to complexity theory, not to the thesis.

examples.question: The lambda term (λn.n+1) 5 is given. Reduce it to a number. Then use the Church-Turing thesis to state what follows about a Turing machine computing f(5).
steps: 1. The term applies the function λn.n+1 to the argument 5. The bound variable is n.
4. The reduction used finitely many exact substitution and arithmetic steps, so f is effectively computable.
5. By the Church-Turing thesis, some Turing machine computes f. With input 5 encoded on its tape, it halts with output 6 encoded on its tape.
examples.answer: The term reduces to 6, and the thesis guarantees that a Turing machine computes f(5)=6.

traps: The thesis is not a theorem. Writing 'by the Church-Turing theorem' loses marks; write thesis or hypothesis.
One simulation or one example does not prove the thesis. The evidence is the agreement of independent models.
'Effectively computable' means a finite mechanical procedure, not fast or practical. A function can be computable and still need enormous time.
Equivalence of two formal models is a theorem. The thesis is the separate claim that the formal class matches the informal idea.
A Turing-complete language can simulate a Turing machine, but it does not make every program efficient. Do not mix computability with complexity.

quiz.q: State the Church-Turing thesis in one sentence.
quiz.a: Every effectively computable function can be computed by a Turing machine.

quiz.q: Why can the thesis not be proved as a theorem?
quiz.a: It links a formal model to the informal idea of effective computability. That informal idea has no independent formal definition, so a formal proof cannot establish the link.

quiz.q: Name two formal models that define the same class of functions as Turing machines.
quiz.a: Any two of lambda calculus, recursive functions, Post systems.

quiz.q: Reduce (λn.n+1) 7, then state the conclusion from the thesis.
quiz.a: Substitute 7 for n: 7+1=8. The function is effectively computable, so by the thesis some Turing machine computes f(7)=8.

quiz.q: An algorithm lists all factors of a number by testing 1 to n. What does the thesis guarantee?
quiz.a: Some Turing machine computes the same function. You do not need to write tape-level rules to know a Turing machine exists.

quiz.q: Lambda calculus equals Turing machines is a proved theorem. Why does that not prove the Church-Turing thesis?
quiz.a: The theorem compares two formal systems. The thesis claims that those formal systems capture every possible effective procedure. Equality of two formal models does not rule out an informal procedure outside both.

quiz.q: A student says: 'I simulated one Turing machine in lambda calculus, so the thesis is proved.' Explain the error.
quiz.a: One simulation proves only that one machine has a lambda term. The thesis is a universal claim about all effective procedures. It needs broad evidence, not one example.

quiz.q: What would a genuine counterexample to the thesis look like?
quiz.a: An exact finite mechanical procedure for a function that no Turing machine computes. A slow procedure, or one Turing machine, is not a counterexample.

beyond: Not for the exam. The lambda calculus became the core of functional programming languages such as Haskell and OCaml. Proof assistants use calculi closely related to it to check mathematical proofs. Researchers study restricted models and quantum models to ask what changes when physics changes. Search for 'lambda calculus', 'Church-Turing thesis', 'computability', and 'Turing completeness'.
